Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Navy Officer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Crowding: Crowded places, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Avoid Friends: avoid seeing friends, Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others

Vignette:
Michael, a 34-year-old Navy Officer, sits stiffly in the chair, his uniform immaculate but his posture betraying a tension that seems etched into his frame. It has been eight months since his unit’s humanitarian deployment, and the man his wife describes as once being the life of every party has become a quiet, distant presence in their home. The official reports called the event a flash flood and subsequent mudslide, a catastrophic act of nature. For Michael, it remains a series of disjointed, silent images that ambush him without warning.

The mission had been going well. His team was helping rebuild a coastal village, and to show their gratitude, the community held a small celebration in a low-lying hall near the riverbank. The air was thick with the sweet, fermented scent of a local spirit being passed around. Michael remembers the laughter, the music, and then the sudden, torrential rain. The lights flickered and died, plunging the crowded room into absolute darkness. The sound that followed wasn't of water, but of the earth giving way—a deep, grinding roar. He was thrown against a wall as the floor buckled and the roof collapsed. Pinned by a heavy beam, with his legs submerged in cold, rising mud, he could only listen to the chaos around him. The memory doesn't come back to him as a story, but as searingly clear snapshots: the wide, terrified eyes of a woman just before the lights went out; the splintered wood of the ceiling inches from his face; the glint of a belt buckle in the murky water. When these images surface, whether he’s in a briefing or at the dinner table, his body involuntarily follows. His back arches and his legs tense, a physical echo of the crushing weight, his body reenacting the moment he was trapped.

In the months since his return, Michael has systematically dismantled his own life. He had come to believe he no longer belonged anywhere, a ghost haunting his own home and naval base. The camaraderie he once cherished with his unit now feels like a language he no longer speaks. He makes excuses to avoid after-work drinks with his friends, the faintest smell of alcohol on someone’s breath enough to make his stomach clench and his palms sweat. He feels profoundly set apart from them, convinced their laughter and easy conversation are worlds away from the silent, terrifying images that occupy his mind. At home, he can no longer sleep in the dark, a small lamp now a permanent fixture on his nightstand. His wife has learned not to suggest trips to the mall or a busy restaurant; the press of a crowd makes him agitated and short-tempered, and he will find any reason to leave.

This careful avoidance has created a sterile, empty space where his life used to be. He feels a profound sense of isolation, a chasm between himself and everyone he loves. He carries a deep, unspoken conviction that he deserves this suffering. As an officer, he was responsible for his people and for the civilians they were there to help. He tells himself, in quiet, punishing moments late at night, that a better leader would have anticipated the danger, would have acted faster, would have saved more people. This thought has calcified into a core belief: his current misery is a just penance for his failure. The happy, confident man he once was feels like a complete stranger, a memory of a person lost forever in the mud. When he tries to explain it to his wife, the words falter. He tells her the whole event feels unreal, like a grotesque film he once saw. It’s too extreme, too horrific to have actually happened to him.

It was a formal performance review that finally pushed him to seek help. His commanding officer, a man he deeply respected, noted his withdrawal and the stark change in his engagement with his duties. That professional rebuke, coupled with his wife’s tearful admission that she felt she was living with a stranger, broke through his wall of avoidance. He is here now, not out of a firm belief he can be fixed, but out of a desperate, flickering hope that he can stop his world from shrinking any further.
